One quick flag before the letter: a physician's order is important evidence, but Medicare inpatient status hinges on the admitting order formally designating her as *inpatient* (versus observation), generally supported by the expectation of a stay spanning two midnights. So the letter pushes for exactly that — a formal inpatient admission order or a physician advisor review — rather than only citing the emergency placement order. That framing gives you the best shot.

**URGENT — Request for Inpatient Status Designation and Appeal of Observation/Outpatient Classification**

[Date]
[Case Manager Name]
[Hospital Name and Address]

Re: [Mother's full name], DOB [date], MRN/Account # [number]

Dear [Case Manager Name],

I am writing on behalf of my mother, [name], who is scheduled for transfer to [nursing facility name] today at 2:00 PM. I am formally protesting her current status classification and requesting an immediate review before discharge.

On [date], Dr. [name] signed an emergency direct placement order for my mother's admission and subsequent skilled nursing facility placement. This order reflects a physician's medical judgment that her condition required hospital-level care, not outpatient observation. I request that her stay be designated as inpatient consistent with that order.

As you know, Medicare coverage of skilled nursing facility care under Part A requires a qualifying inpatient hospital stay of at least three consecutive midnights (42 CFR § 409.30). If my mother is discharged classified as observation/outpatient, she will be denied SNF coverage and our family will face costs we cannot bear — an outcome caused by a billing classification, not by her medical condition.

I therefore request, before the 2:00 PM transfer:

1. Immediate review of her status by the hospital's Utilization Review Committee and physician advisor, per the Condition Code 44 process if applicable;
2. A formal inpatient admission order from the treating physician, or written explanation of why inpatient criteria are not met;
3. Issuance of all required notices, including the Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice (MOON) if observation status is maintained, and an Important Message from Medicare (IM) describing our appeal rights;
4. Documentation of this request in her medical record, and a written response before discharge.

Please also note that we intend to pursue an expedited appeal through the Beneficiary and Family Centered Care Quality Improvement Organization (BFCC-QIO) if the classification is not corrected, and we ask that the transfer not proceed until this review is complete.

I can be reached immediately at [phone]. Time is critical — please contact me before any discharge action is taken.

Sincerely,
[Your name], [relationship/healthcare proxy if applicable]
[Address, phone, email]

---

**FORMAL PROTEST — Inpatient Status Established by Signed Physician Order**

[Date]
[Case Manager Name]
[Hospital Name and Address]

Re: [Mother's full name], DOB [date], MRN/Account # [number]

Dear [Case Manager Name],

I am writing to formally protest the classification of my mother's hospital stay prior to her scheduled transfer to [nursing facility name] today at 2:00 PM.

On [date], Dr. [name] signed an emergency direct placement order for my mother. That signed order constitutes the physician's formal determination that she required and received inpatient hospital care. Under Medicare's two-midnight rule and 42 CFR § 412.3, a stay is inpatient when the admitting practitioner orders inpatient admission based on the expectation that the patient requires hospital care — which is exactly what Dr. [name]'s signed emergency order documents. The stay was therefore inpatient care as a matter of the medical record, and any classification of it as observation or outpatient contradicts the physician's own signed order.

This classification carries direct consequences: Medicare Part A covers skilled nursing facility care only following a qualifying inpatient stay of three or more consecutive midnights (42 CFR § 409.30). My mother met that requirement as an inpatient. Reclassifying her stay as observation would strip her of Part A SNF coverage based on a billing label rather than the documented medical facts, and would impose catastrophic costs on our family.

Accordingly, before the 2:00 PM transfer, I demand that the hospital:

1. Recognize the stay as inpatient consistent with Dr. [name]'s signed emergency direct placement order, and code and bill it accordingly;
2. Provide written confirmation of inpatient status, or a written explanation signed by the physician advisor identifying any basis for departing from the treating physician's order;
3. Issue any notices required if the hospital nonetheless maintains an observation classification, including the MOON and the Important Message from Medicare, so our appeal rights are preserved;
4. Document this protest in her medical record and provide me a copy of the complete record, including the signed order and all status-determination documentation.

If the hospital does not correct the classification, we will immediately pursue an expedited appeal with the BFCC-QIO and will raise the signed order as the controlling evidence of inpatient status. I ask that the transfer be held until this is resolved.

I am available now at [phone]. Please respond in writing before any discharge action is taken.

Sincerely,
[Your name], [relationship/healthcare proxy]
[Address, phone, email]

---

One thing to keep in your back pocket: if the case manager responds that the stay was never formally ordered as *inpatient* at admission, ask directly for the physician advisor to review and convert it (the Condition Code 44 route) — that request pairs naturally with this letter and is often how these get resolved.

**FORMAL PROTEST — Stay Constitutes Inpatient Care Per Signed Physician Order**

[Date]
[Case Manager Name]
[Hospital Name and Address]

Re: [Mother's full name], DOB [date], MRN/Account # [number]

Dear [Case Manager Name],

This letter is a formal protest of the classification of my mother's hospital stay. Her transfer to [nursing facility name] is scheduled for today at 2:00 PM.

On [date], Dr. [name] signed an emergency direct placement order for my mother. That signed order establishes that her stay was inpatient care. It is the treating physician's documented, signed determination that she required hospital admission, and it is part of her medical record. Any classification of this stay as observation or outpatient is contrary to the physician's signed order and is hereby disputed.

As an inpatient, my mother has satisfied the three-midnight qualifying stay requirement for Medicare Part A skilled nursing facility coverage under 42 CFR § 409.30. She is entitled to Part A coverage of her nursing facility care. Denying that coverage based on a classification that contradicts the treating physician's signed order would cause our family immediate and severe financial harm.

Before the 2:00 PM transfer, I demand that the hospital:

1. Confirm in writing that the stay is classified and billed as inpatient, consistent with Dr. [name]'s signed order;
2. If the hospital disputes this, provide a written explanation, signed by the physician advisor, of the basis for classifying the stay contrary to the treating physician's signed order;
3. Issue the Important Message from Medicare and any other required notices so our appeal rights are fully preserved;
4. Enter this protest into her medical record and provide me a complete copy of the record, including the signed order.

We will pursue an expedited appeal with the BFCC-QIO immediately if the inpatient classification is not confirmed, and the signed order will be the central evidence in that appeal. I request that the transfer be held pending resolution.

I am available now at [phone]. Respond in writing before any discharge action is taken.

Sincerely,
[Your name], [relationship/healthcare proxy]
[Address, phone, email]

---

Two moves to make in parallel, because the letter alone won't stop the clock: call your state's BFCC-QIO (Livanta or Acentra) and request an expedited appeal by phone — that can hold the discharge — and ask the case manager point-blank for the physician advisor to review and convert her status before 2:00 PM. **FORMAL PROTEST — Inpatient Status Per Signed Physician Order**

[Date]
[Case Manager Name]
[Hospital Name and Address]

Re: [Mother's full name], DOB [date], MRN/Account # [number]

Dear [Case Manager Name],

This letter is a formal protest regarding the classification of my mother's hospital stay, in advance of her scheduled transfer to [nursing facility name] today at 2:00 PM.

On [date], Dr. [name] signed an emergency direct placement order for my mother. That order directed her inpatient admission and placement, and it is the physician's signed determination that her stay was inpatient hospital care. It is part of her permanent medical record, and it controls how this stay must be classified. The stay was inpatient care, as ordered in writing by her treating physician.

Because her stay was inpatient and spanned three or more consecutive midnights, she has satisfied the qualifying stay requirement for Medicare Part A skilled nursing facility coverage under 42 CFR § 409.30. She is entitled to Part A coverage of her nursing facility care beginning today.

Accordingly, before the 2:00 PM transfer, I require that the hospital:

1. Classify and bill the stay as inpatient, consistent with Dr. [name]'s signed emergency direct placement order, and confirm this to me in writing;
2. Provide written confirmation of inpatient status to [nursing facility name] so that Medicare Part A coverage of her care there is not interrupted;
3. Issue the Important Message from Medicare and preserve all of our appeal rights;
4. Enter this protest into her medical record and provide me a complete copy of the record, including the signed order.

Any classification of this stay as observation or outpatient would contradict the treating physician's signed order and will be appealed immediately to the BFCC-QIO on an expedited basis, with the signed order as the central evidence.

The doctor ordered inpatient care in writing. I expect the hospital's records to reflect exactly that. I am available now at [phone]. Please respond in writing before any discharge action is taken.

Sincerely,
[Your name], [relationship/healthcare proxy]
[Address, phone, email]

---
